Kennedy Space Center LC-39A, 1969-07-16 13:32 UTC. Saturn V — the largest, most powerful rocket to fly successfully (until Starship's first orbital flight) — lifts the Apollo 11 stack of CSM Columbia + LM Eagle + Armstrong + Aldrin + Collins.

S-IVB third-stage burn at 2h 44m, accelerating the stack from its 186 × 183 km Earth parking orbit to 10.83 km/s — just short of Earth's escape velocity, on a long ellipse reaching out to the Moon. Begins the 3-day translunar coast.
Mid-cruise trajectory tweak. Mission planning called for 4 MCCs; only MCC-2 was needed because the TLI was precise enough that the other three were waived.

1969-07-19. 357-second SPS engine burn at the Moon's far side (out of Earth radio contact) braked the CSM into a 113 × 313 km lunar orbit. The crew waited for Earth re-acquisition to confirm LOI success.

1969-07-20 20:05 UTC. After undocking from Columbia, Eagle began powered descent from 15 km altitude to the surface. The famous 1201 + 1202 program alarms — guidance computer overflows — were judged 'GO' by 24-year-old Steve Bales at Mission Control. Armstrong manually targeted past a boulder field, landing with <30 seconds of fuel reserve.

1969-07-21 17:54 UTC. After 21h 36m on the lunar surface — including the 2h 31m EVA — the ascent stage lifted off from Tranquility Base. The ascent engine was a one-shot pressure-fed bipropellant with no backup; if it failed, the crew was permanently stranded.
1969-07-22. SPS engine burn departing lunar orbit. Set Apollo 11 on course back to Earth.

1969-07-24 16:50 UTC. Command Module splashed down 1,440 km southwest of Honolulu, recovered by USS Hornet. The crew was quarantined for 3 weeks — a NASA precaution against unknown lunar pathogens — before being released to a world that had watched humans walk on the Moon — a TV audience of 650 million.
First humans on another celestial body

Apollo 11 was the flight the whole program was built to make — the one that had to work. For eight years and $25 billion, everything NASA did came down, in the end, to getting two people onto this particular patch of grey dust and back off it alive. When Armstrong called "the Eagle has landed," the Cold-War race that opened with a beeping sphere over American cities was effectively over. What's easy to forget now is how little margin there was: the crew came down with seconds of fuel to spare, past a boulder field the maps hadn't shown, riding a guidance computer that was throwing alarms the whole way. It worked anyway — and for one night, a fifth of the species watched the same thing at the same time.

The mission that fulfilled Kennedy's 1961 commitment to put a man on the Moon by the end of the decade. Armstrong and Aldrin spent 21 hours 36 minutes on the lunar surface — 2.5 hours of EVA, 21.55 kg of samples, and a single commemorative plaque. The laser retroreflector they installed at Mare Tranquillitatis still receives pulses today, measuring the Earth-Moon distance to millimetre precision. The mission was watched live by ~600 million people, one fifth of humanity at the time.
